$6.3 Billion Stolen in 20 Minutes: How the Biggest Crypto Hack Ever Happened

2026-11-04

Subscribe for one money story a week

About this video

On October 29, 2026, hackers drained about $6.3 billion from Binance, the world's biggest crypto exchange, in about 20 minutes. It's the largest crypto theft ever recorded, roughly four times the old record. Here's how it happened, who the FBI says did it, who pays for it, and what it means for anyone who keeps money on an exchange. What we know (as of November 1, 2026): - Binance's first findings: a compromised engineer's laptop gave access to a service container; Binance says it found no evidence its private keys leaked; its co-CEO says the attack was more complex - TRM Labs: staging began well before the theft; signatures obtained in advance, executed in one burst - FBI (Oct 31): North Korea is responsible (a group known as TraderTraitor); funds are being converted mostly into Ethereum - About $3 billion frozen with partners including Tether and Circle (Binance) - Binance says it will absorb the losses (SAFU fund, futures insurance fund, treasury): about 90% covered Saturday, 95% Sunday - Withdrawals resumed in phases on November 1 Details may still change; Binance says a full incident report will follow. 0:00 Intro: $6.3 billion in 20 minutes 0:12 How big is this? 0:43 Hot wallets vs cold storage 1:09 How they got in 1:35 Planned in advance 1:55 Hiding the money 2:29 Who did it: North Korea 3:07 Who pays for it? 3:37 Can people withdraw? 3:56 What it did to bitcoin 4:10 What it means for you 4:44 Recap Sources: Binance statements; FBI statement (Oct 31, 2026); TRM Labs; Chainalysis Crypto Crime report (Dec 2025); UN Panel of Experts; CNBC (Oct 31 / Nov 1, 2026); TechCrunch (Nov 1, 2026); NBC News; Bloomberg; CoinDesk; The Block; Decrypt and Benzinga (largest crypto hacks); FBI PSA I-022625-PSA (Bybit, 2025). Transcript

$6.3 billion. Gone, in about 20 minutes. This is the biggest crypto theft in history. Here's exactly how it happened, who did it, and what it means for anyone who keeps money on an exchange. First, how big is this? Here are the biggest crypto thefts ever. Mt. Gox in 2014, about 460 million dollars. Poly Network and Ronin, a little over 600 million each. Bybit in 2025, about 1.5 billion. And Binance: about $6.3 billion. That's roughly four times the old record. It's even more than North Korea stole in all of 2025, which was already a record at about 2.02 billion dollars. To understand how it happened, you need to know where an exchange keeps your crypto. When you buy on an exchange, the coins usually sit in wallets the exchange controls, not you. Most of it is kept in cold storage: offline, much harder to reach. But some has to stay online, in so-called hot wallets, so the exchange can pay out withdrawals quickly. This time, it was the hot wallets that were drained. That's where the attackers aimed. So how did they get in? Binance's first findings point to one engineer's laptop. Hackers compromised it, and that gave them access to a service container, a piece of the exchange's internal systems. Binance says it has found no evidence that its private keys, the master passwords to its wallets, leaked. But Binance's co-CEO, Richard Teng, has said the attack was more complex than one engineer's access. The full incident report is still to come. What we do know is that this was planned. Blockchain investigators at TRM Labs found the staging started well before the theft. Then it all happened at once. In TRM's words: signatures obtained in advance, then executed in one burst. The money moved across about 10 different blockchains, and most of it was gone in about 20 minutes. Step two for any thief is hiding the money. The stolen coins included all kinds of tokens. According to the FBI, the hackers have been converting them mostly into Ethereum, and it expects more laundering steps to follow. Here's why that matters. Some crypto can be frozen. Stablecoins like Tether and USDC are run by companies that can block stolen coins. Bitcoin and Ethereum have no company in charge. No one can freeze them. So far, Binance says about $3 billion has been frozen with help from partners including Tether and Circle. Who did it? On October 31st, the FBI said North Korea was responsible, naming a hacking group known as TraderTraitor. Investigators say the attack follows the same playbook as the Bybit hack in 2025 and the KelpDAO hack this April, right down to how the attackers funded their wallets. And this is a pattern. According to Chainalysis, North Korea-linked hackers stole about 2.02 billion dollars in crypto in 2025, a record. That was about 59% of all the crypto stolen worldwide that year. United Nations experts have said this stolen money helps fund the country's weapons programs. So who pays? Binance says it will absorb the losses, not its customers. It's using its emergency fund for users, called SAFU, part of its futures insurance fund, and money from its own treasury. On Saturday, Binance said about 90% of the affected assets were covered. By Sunday, it said 95%. The 10 biggest coins, including bitcoin and ether, are fully backed, it says. The rest are smaller tokens it's still buying back. Right after the hack, Binance paused deposits and withdrawals. On Sunday, November 1st, withdrawals started coming back in phases: first the Bitcoin network, then Ethereum and BNB Smart Chain. Binance warned of delays, and says a fuller incident report will follow once its investigation is done. The news hit the whole market. The night of the hack, bitcoin briefly fell below $77,000. It was a scare, not a collapse, but it shows how much of crypto runs through a single exchange. So what does this mean for you? We don't give financial advice, but this hack teaches four things. One: when your crypto sits on an exchange, the exchange holds the keys. You're trusting its security. Two: an exchange's reserves and insurance funds matter. They're why Binance customers may not lose money this time. Three: after every big hack, scammers pretend to be support staff. Real support will never ask for your password or your recovery phrase. Four: holding crypto yourself removes the exchange risk, but if you lose your own keys, nobody can get them back. Let's recap. About $6.3 billion, the biggest crypto theft ever, taken in one planned burst of about 20 minutes. The FBI says North Korea did it. And Binance says it has covered 95% so far, with its own money. Would you keep your crypto on an exchange after this? Tell me in the comments, and subscribe so you don't miss the full incident report when it comes out. This video is for education only.
